notes.definition: Acids react with some metals to produce a salt and hydrogen: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. At Higher tier, these are redox reactions in which the metal atoms lose electrons and the hydrogen ions gain electrons.
explanation: Metals that are above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas. The general word equation is metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. At GCSE you need to know the reactions of magnesium, zinc and iron with dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute sulfuric acid. Copper is below hydrogen, so it does not react with these dilute acids.

The name of the salt has two parts. The first part comes from the metal and the second part comes from the acid. Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides and sulfuric acid makes sulfates. For example, magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen, and zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + hydrogen. As symbol equations: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) and Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g). Iron forms iron(II) salts in these reactions: Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) → FeCl₂(aq) + H₂(g).

When a metal reacts with an acid you see fizzing (effervescence) as bubbles of hydrogen are given off, the metal gets smaller and eventually disappears if the acid is in excess, and the mixture gets warmer because the reaction is exothermic. Magnesium reacts vigorously, zinc steadily and iron slowly, which matches their order in the reactivity series. You can test the gas with a lighted splint: hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop.

You can compare how quickly metals react with acid by collecting the hydrogen in a gas syringe or an upturned measuring cylinder and measuring the volume every few seconds. For a fair comparison, keep the acid concentration, acid volume, temperature and the mass and surface area of the metal the same. The reaction slows down and stops when either the metal or the acid has been used up.

Higher tier: reactions of metals with acids are redox reactions. In solution, acids produce hydrogen ions, H⁺(aq). The chloride or sulfate ions do not change, so they are spectator ions. The ionic equation for magnesium with any dilute acid is Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g). Magnesium atoms lose two electrons and are oxidised (Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻). Hydrogen ions gain electrons and are reduced (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂). The same pattern applies to zinc and iron: Zn + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂ and Fe + 2H⁺ → Fe²⁺ + H₂.
keyFacts: Hydrochloric acid produces chloride salts; sulfuric acid produces sulfate salts.
Magnesium reacts vigorously, zinc steadily and iron slowly with dilute acids; copper does not react.
Test for hydrogen: a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
Higher: the metal is oxidised (loses electrons) and the hydrogen ions are reduced (gain electrons).
Higher: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g); chloride and sulfate ions are spectator ions.

keyTerms.definition: A substance that produces hydrogen ions, H⁺, in aqueous solution, such as hydrochloric acid or sulfuric acid.
A compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal, such as zinc sulfate.
Fizzing caused by bubbles of gas being produced in a liquid.
A salt made from hydrochloric acid, containing Cl⁻ ions.
A salt made from sulfuric acid, containing SO₄²⁻ ions.
A reaction in which one species is oxidised (loses electrons) and another is reduced (gains electrons).

workedExamples.title: Naming the salt and writing the equation
workedExamples.question: Zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Name the products and write a balanced symbol equation with state symbols.
steps: Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, so the salt is zinc chloride.
Zinc forms Zn²⁺ and chloride is Cl⁻, so the formula is ZnCl₂.
Zn + HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ needs 2HCl to balance the H and Cl atoms.
Add state symbols: zinc is solid, acid and salt are aqueous, hydrogen is a gas.
workedExamples.answer: Zinc chloride and hydrogen. Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)

workedExamples.title: Mean rate of gas production
workedExamples.question: A piece of magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid. 60 cm³ of hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe in 40 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.
steps: Mean rate = volume of gas ÷ time.

workedExamples.title: Higher: identifying oxidation and reduction
workedExamples.question: Iron reacts with dilute sulfuric acid: Fe(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + H₂(g). Write the ionic equation and identify the species oxidised and reduced.
steps: Split the aqueous ionic substances into ions: Fe + 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → Fe²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + H₂.
Sulfate ions are unchanged, so they are spectator ions.
Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻: iron loses electrons, so iron is oxidised.
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂: hydrogen ions gain electrons, so H⁺ is reduced.
workedExamples.answer: Fe(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + H₂(g); iron is oxidised, hydrogen ions are reduced.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all metals react with acids.
misconceptions.right: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids. Copper, silver and gold do not.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think metal + acid gives a salt and water.
misconceptions.right: Metal + acid gives a salt and hydrogen. Salt and water are produced when an acid reacts with a base or alkali.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the gas given off is oxygen or carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.right: The gas is hydrogen, which comes from the acid. Carbon dioxide is only produced when acids react with carbonates.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the hydrogen ions are oxidised because hydrogen gas is produced.
misconceptions.right: Higher: hydrogen ions gain electrons (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂), so they are reduced. The metal is oxidised.

realWorld: Acid rain slowly reacts with iron and zinc on buildings and structures, corroding them and releasing hydrogen.
Zinc and dilute sulfuric acid were used to make hydrogen to fill early balloons.
Some descaling products are acidic, so they should not be left on metal surfaces such as zinc-coated (galvanised) steel.
higherTier: Reactions of metals with acids are redox reactions: explain this in terms of gain and loss of electrons.
The metal atom loses electrons and is oxidised, for example Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.
Hydrogen ions gain electrons and are reduced: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
Ionic equation: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g). Chloride and sulfate ions are spectator ions.
Identify which species are oxidised and which are reduced in given chemical equations.
examTips: Remember: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Do not write water as a product.
Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides; sulfuric acid gives sulfates. Spell sulfate with an f.
Balance carefully: hydrochloric acid needs 2HCl for Mg, Zn and Fe, but sulfuric acid needs only one H₂SO₄.
Describe observations as fizzing or bubbles, metal getting smaller, and the mixture getting warm.
Higher: name species precisely: 'magnesium atoms are oxidised; hydrogen ions are reduced'.
summary: Metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen.
Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides; sulfuric acid gives sulfates.
Magnesium reacts vigorously, zinc steadily, iron slowly; copper does not react.
Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.
Higher: the metal is oxidised (loses electrons) and H⁺ ions are reduced (gain electrons).

questions.question: Which gas is produced when magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Carbon dioxide forms only with carbonates, and chlorine is not released.

questions.question: What is the test for hydrogen gas?
options: It burns with a squeaky pop when a lighted splint is held near
markScheme: 1 mark: lighted splint gives a squeaky pop
questions.explanation: A glowing splint relighting is the test for oxygen, limewater is for carbon dioxide, and bleaching litmus is the test for chlorine.

questions.question: Which salt is produced when zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid makes chloride salts. Sulfates come from sulfuric acid.

questions.question: Iron reacts with dilute sulfuric acid. What are the products?
questions.explanation: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen, and sulfuric acid makes sulfates. Water is a product when acids react with bases, not metals.

questions.question: Which is the balanced symbol equation for magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Magnesium chloride is MgCl₂ (Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻) and hydrogen gas is H₂, so 2HCl are needed. MgCl is an incorrect formula.

questions.question: Equal-sized pieces of four metals are added to the same dilute hydrochloric acid. Which metal produces bubbles fastest?
questions.explanation: Magnesium is the most reactive of these. Zinc reacts steadily, iron slowly and copper not at all.

questions.question: A student adds a large piece of zinc to a small volume of dilute sulfuric acid. After a while the fizzing stops but some zinc is left. Why did the fizzing stop?
options: The zinc became coated in hydrogen
The zinc sulfate stopped the reaction
markScheme: 1 mark: all the acid had been used up (the zinc was in excess)
questions.explanation: There was more zinc than the acid could react with, so the acid was used up first. The zinc left over is in excess.

questions.question:
Zn(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + H₂(g)
Which statement is correct?
options: Zinc is reduced and hydrogen ions are oxidised
Zinc is oxidised and hydrogen ions are reduced
Both zinc and hydrogen ions are oxidised
markScheme: 1 mark: zinc is oxidised and hydrogen ions are reduced
questions.explanation: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (loss of electrons, oxidation). 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (gain of electrons, reduction).

questions.question: Which half equation shows what happens to the hydrogen ions when a metal reacts with an acid?
questions.explanation: Two H⁺ ions each gain one electron to form a hydrogen molecule. The second option is the reverse; the third does not balance for charge; the fourth does not balance for atoms.

questions.question: Which mixture would not produce hydrogen?
markScheme: 1 mark: copper and dilute hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not react with dilute acids. The other three metals are above hydrogen.

questions.question: A student added 0.50 g of magnesium ribbon to some hydrochloric acid. When the fizzing stopped, 0.14 g of magnesium was left. Calculate the mass of magnesium that reacted.
questions.explanation: Mass reacted = starting mass − mass left over = 0.50 − 0.14 = 0.36 g. The acid must have been used up first.

questions.question:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of magnesium chloride, MgCl₂.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Mg = 24, Cl = 35.5
questions.explanation: There are two chlorine atoms: 2 × 35.5 = 71. 24 + 71 = 95.

questions.question: Zinc reacts with sulfuric acid. 60 cm³ of hydrogen is collected in 40 s. Calculate the mean rate of hydrogen production.
questions.explanation: Mean rate = volume ÷ time = 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 cm³/s.

questions.question:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of zinc sulfate, ZnSO₄.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Zn = 65, S = 32, O = 16
questions.explanation: 65 + 32 + 64 = 161. Remember the 4 oxygen atoms in the sulfate group.

questions.question:
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
In this reaction, 24 g of magnesium produces 95 g of magnesium chloride. Calculate the mass of magnesium chloride produced when 0.36 g of magnesium reacts completely. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.explanation: The ratio of masses is fixed: 0.36 ÷ 24 = 0.015, and 0.015 × 95 = 1.425 g, which rounds to 1.43 g.

questions.question:
Complete the word equation:
zinc + sulfuric acid → ________ + ________
questions.explanation: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Sulfuric acid gives sulfate salts.

questions.question: Name the salt formed when magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid.
questions.explanation: The metal gives the first part of the name and hydrochloric acid gives 'chloride'.

questions.question: A piece of magnesium ribbon is dropped into a test tube of dilute hydrochloric acid. Describe two observations.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: fizzing / bubbles; magnesium gets smaller / disappears; test tube gets warm
questions.explanation: Observations describe what you see or feel. 'Hydrogen is produced' is not an observation; 'bubbles' is.

questions.question: Iron reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form iron(II) sulfate, FeSO₄, and hydrogen. Write a balanced symbol equation, including state symbols.
questions.explanation: This equation is already balanced with one of each substance. The salt dissolves in water, so it is (aq).

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation, including state symbols, for the reaction of zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid.
questions.explanation: Zinc chloride is ZnCl₂, so two HCl are needed to supply 2 Cl and 2 H (which form H₂).

questions.question: Write the ionic equation, including state symbols, for the reaction between magnesium and dilute hydrochloric acid.
questions.explanation: Chloride ions are spectator ions and are left out. Charge balances: 2+ on each side.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of electrons, why the reaction between zinc and dilute sulfuric acid is a redox reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: zinc atoms lose (two) electrons to form Zn²⁺ ions, so zinc is oxidised
1 mark: hydrogen ions gain electrons to form hydrogen (H₂), so H⁺ ions are reduced
1 mark: oxidation and reduction happen at the same time / electrons are transferred from zinc to hydrogen ions
questions.explanation: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. The sulfate ions are spectators and do not change.

questions.question: Explain why chloride ions are not included in the ionic equation for the reaction between iron and hydrochloric acid.
markScheme: 1 mark: they are spectator ions / they do not change during the reaction
questions.explanation: Cl⁻ ions are in solution at the start (from HCl) and at the end (in FeCl₂ solution), unchanged.

questions.question: Describe a method to compare how quickly magnesium, zinc and iron react with dilute hydrochloric acid by measuring the hydrogen produced. Include how you would make it a fair test, the expected results and how to test the gas.
markScheme: Indicative content: measure a fixed volume (e.g. 25 cm³) of the same concentration of hydrochloric acid into a conical flask; add a known mass of metal with the same surface area (e.g. all powder); quickly fit a bung with a delivery tube to a gas syringe (or upturned measuring cylinder in water); start a stop clock; record the volume of gas every 10 or 20 s, or the volume after a fixed time; keep temperature the same; repeat for each metal; calculate the mean rate; expect magnesium fastest, then zinc, then iron slowest; test the gas with a lighted splint: squeaky pop shows hydrogen; wear eye protection.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically ordered method with control of variables, a way to measure gas volume over time, a correct prediction and the hydrogen test.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with some control variables and measurement, may lack the prediction or the gas test.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic statements such as add metals to acid and see which bubbles most.
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the metal; the dependent variable is the volume of hydrogen (or rate). Keeping acid concentration, volume, temperature and the metal's mass and surface area the same makes it fair.

questions.question:
Iron reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid:
Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) → FeCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Explain this reaction in terms of oxidation and reduction. Include the ionic equation and two half equations.
markScheme: Indicative content: HCl and FeCl₂ are ionic in solution: H⁺, Cl⁻ and Fe²⁺; chloride ions are spectator ions; ionic equation Fe(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + H₂(g); half equations Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (loss of electrons, oxidation) and 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (gain of electrons, reduction); iron atoms are oxidised and hydrogen ions are reduced; electrons transfer from iron to hydrogen ions, so it is a redox reaction.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct ionic equation and half equations with correct identification of the species oxidised and reduced.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): partial answer, for example iron is oxidised, with limited use of equations.
questions.explanation: Removing the spectator Cl⁻ ions shows the real change: electrons pass from Fe atoms to H⁺ ions.

questions.question:
A student reacted equal masses of magnesium powder and zinc powder with 25 cm³ portions of the same hydrochloric acid. The acid was used up in both reactions. Volumes of hydrogen collected:
Time (s): 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100
Magnesium (cm³): 0, 40, 62, 70, 72, 72
Zinc (cm³): 0, 12, 23, 33, 42, 50
Compare the two reactions and explain what the results show.
markScheme: Indicative content: magnesium produces gas faster at the start (40 cm³ in the first 20 s compared with 12 cm³ for zinc, about 3 times as fast); magnesium reaction finishes by about 80 s (volume stays at 72 cm³) while zinc is still producing gas at 100 s; so magnesium is more reactive than zinc; this matches the reactivity series; the zinc reaction would eventually produce the same final volume because the same amount of acid was used up in both; rate of magnesium slows as acid is used up.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear comparison using data from the table, a correct conclusion about reactivity and an explanation of the final volume or slowing rate.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statement that magnesium is faster or more reactive, with little use of data.
questions.explanation: The initial rate (gradient) compares reactivity. The final volume depends on the limiting reactant: here the acid, which was the same in both.

questions.question: Magnesium is added to dilute sulfuric acid. Which list gives all the products?
options: Magnesium sulfate, water and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Water forms with bases, and carbon dioxide only forms with carbonates.
